text: Once you know a workload's RTO and RPO, there are really only two patterns on the table for meeting them across regions: active-passive and active-active. Each one trades cost against speed in a different place, and picking between them is a lot easier once you stop thinking of it as a preference and start thinking of it as the direct consequence of the numbers from the last lesson.

Active-passive is the simpler shape: one region, the primary, serves all live traffic. The secondary is a standby that doesn't take user traffic until failover — and it can sit at three different tiers. Cold or pilot-light keeps only the data current and provisions compute after disaster is declared. Warm standby keeps the full stack running at reduced capacity. Hot standby runs at full capacity already, just not receiving traffic.

What makes active-passive attractive is that replication only flows one direction, so two regions never disagree about a record's state. What makes it slower is everything failover requires: detecting the outage, promoting the secondary's data store, redirecting traffic through DNS, and scaling up compute for anything short of a hot standby. Because that replication is rarely perfectly synchronous, there's almost always a small window of writes that never made it across — that gap is the real RPO, whatever the documentation says.

Active-active flips the shape: both regions serve live traffic at once, behind some form of global traffic distribution, and if one fails, the others simply absorb its load — there's no standby to promote. That gets failover down to seconds and removes most of the replication-lag gap. But it creates a problem active-passive never has: if the same record can be written in either region at once, something has to resolve that conflict, and that's genuine distributed-systems engineering, not a diagram exercise.

Active-active also costs more by design, since both regions run full capacity continuously, failure or not. So the choice comes down to the targets: hours of RTO and tens of minutes of RPO are well served by a warm active-passive standby at a fraction of the cost. An RTO of seconds with near-zero RPO rules active-passive out, because DNS propagation and promotion alone are too slow — only active-active clears that bar.

Choosing the right pattern on paper is still only half the job. The next lesson covers the half that most organizations skip: actually proving, through a real failover drill, that the pattern you chose delivers the RTO and RPO you designed it for — because an untested DR plan is a guess, not a plan.
